system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2193-11-02 07:22:00 to 2193-11-04 14:53:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted electively for cardiac catheterization due to increased frequency of chest discomfort and new left ventricular wall motion abnormalities on echocardiogram. He was heparin-brided off warfarin and underwent cardiac catheterization, which showed stable coronary artery disease with patent stents and no new interventions required. His warfarin was restarted and adjusted to 4 mg daily with an INR of 2.5 at discharge. Heart failure was managed medically with no acute decompensation. He was discharged home with instructions to monitor weight, follow up with cardiology, and check INR as scheduled.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Chronic combined systolic and diastolic heart failure
Congestive heart failure, unspecified
Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified
Heart valve replaced by other means
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Benign essential hypertension
Automatic implantable cardiac defibrillator in situ
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted last night after a nosebleed that wouldn’t stop. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been having these nosebleeds off and on for months. That night, it started after I got home from the ER. I couldn’t stop it with pressure, so I came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you were in the ER earlier that day for shortness of breath and swelling in your legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I couldn’t walk more than a block without getting winded. They gave me a stronger dose of my water pill and sent me home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they increased your furosemide. Then the nosebleed started later that night. In the ER, your blood pressure dropped briefly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel dizzy or anything. They said it came back up with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your blood count was low—hematocrit of 28.2, down from 38 recently. That’s a significant drop. You got one unit of blood in the ER and were admitted for more monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been tired lately. And I’ve lost about 10 pounds without trying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. We’re worried the nosebleeds and dark stools might be from ongoing blood loss. You’re on warfarin and aspirin for your heart valve and heart disease, but your Plavix was stopped by your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Dr. Lee said to hold it because of the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We’ll keep it on hold. Your labs show mild hyponatremia—low sodium—which can happen when you’re dehydrated from the diuretics and blood loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild and should improve as we correct your volume and transfuse blood. We’re going to give you two more units of red blood cells today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already got one. Why more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your body is still recovering. The first unit helped, but your hemoglobin didn’t rise as expected—likely because you were dehydrated from the diuretics, so your blood was concentrated. Now that we’re replacing volume, we need more blood to fully correct the anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again, Mr. Thompson. You’ve received two more units of blood. Your latest hemoglobin is up to 11.2, which is a good response after the third unit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My nose hasn’t bled since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using saline spray and Afrin to keep the nasal lining moist and prevent re-bleeding. We’ll switch to saline only soon, since Afrin shouldn’t be used long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the dark stools? Could that be from the nosebleeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Blood swallowed from nosebleeds can turn stools dark. But given your weight loss and past history of a duodenal ulcer, we’re concerned there might be a slow GI bleed too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had an ulcer years ago. They said it was from H. pylori.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your recent H. pylori antibody test came back positive. That means you were exposed, but it doesn’t tell us if it’s active now. You were treated before, so this could be a past infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be treated again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Since you have a duodenal ulcer history and symptoms, your PCP will evaluate you as an outpatient. They may repeat the test or do another endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is stable—mild heart enlargement, but lungs are clear. No signs of pneumonia or fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My breathing feels better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your shortness of breath has improved to your baseline. We restarted your usual dose of furosemide today. We held it briefly on admission to avoid over-diuresis with your low blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my heart medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on all your usual meds: lisinopril, metoprolol, atorvastatin, amiodarone, and warfarin. We’ve slightly reduced your warfarin dose to lower bleeding risk while we sort out the nose and GI issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another blood transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re stable now. Your hemoglobin held after the third unit, and you haven’t bled again. We’ll monitor your labs tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Mr. Thompson. Your sodium is now normal, and your blood pressure is stable. Great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. A bit weak, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Physical therapy saw you yesterday. They noted you’re quite deconditioned—low endurance. They recommended rehab, but I understand you declined?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’d rather go home. My daughter will stay with me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll arrange a visiting nurse, home health aide, and a walker. Please weigh yourself daily and call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Ensure you mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, try two supplements a day. You’re a bit malnourished, which could be contributing to your fatigue and weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news, Mr. Thompson. You’re being discharged today. Your nose hasn’t bled, your hemoglobin is stable, and you’re feeling much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the saline nasal spray three times a day in each nostril. Keep taking your medications as listed. We’ve adjusted your warfarin—two 2 mg tablets three times a week, and one 2 mg tablet the other four days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your PCP this week. They’ll check your CBC and INR. They’ll also discuss the weight loss and possible GI workup, including whether you need another endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A nurse will visit you at home, and your daughter should stay with you 24/7 for now. Call us if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or any bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you doing well at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge—any chest pain or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your INR this morning was 2.8—right in the target range. We’re confident you’re safe to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. A nurse will go over your medications one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Dr. Patel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you have your walker and supplies, and your daughter is here to take you home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything’s set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Discharge is official. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted for recurrent epistaxis and acute posthemorrhagic anemia following a hypotensive episode in the emergency department. He had a 10-point hematocrit drop over several months with dark stools and recent weight loss. He received three units of packed red blood cells, with hemoglobin stabilization after the third unit. His warfarin was slightly reduced, and Plavix remained on hold. The nosebleed resolved with conservative management. Mild hyponatremia and hypovolemia, likely due to diuresis and blood loss, resolved. He was evaluated for deconditioning and declined inpatient rehabilitation; home health services and family support were arranged. A GI workup for possible upper GI bleeding and weight loss was planned for outpatient follow-up with his PCP. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to monitor weight, continue nasal saline, and follow up for INR and CBC testing.
